new_body_html:
So what exactly is Achology? Achology, The Academy of Modern Applied Psychology, is an online applied psychology training academy founded in 2017 and based in Scotland. It teaches practical psychology for personal growth and professional helping work through 28 courses organised across seven schools, a collaborative learning community, and a structured certification pathway. It is an independent education provider registered with the UK Register of Learning Providers; it is not a university, and it is not therapy.

What Achology teaches

The curriculum spans seven schools of applied psychology: The School of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), The School of Cognitive Behavioural Psychology (CBP), The School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping, The School of Person-Centred Counselling and Psychology, The School of Mindfulness, Applied Insight and Wisdom (MIW), The School of Mental Health, Wellness and Emotional Resilience, and The School of Personal Growth and Development (PGD). Each school collects courses in one tradition, from beginner introductions to practitioner-level training, all built around applying psychological insight in real life rather than studying it academically. The full curriculum lives on the Achology courses page, and the schools are introduced on the Academy schools page.

The community and how learning works

Achology's courses sit inside a learning community rather than standing alone. Members practise together through daily live events, peer practice sessions, mentorship groups, and discussion spaces, so the skills taught in the courses are rehearsed with real people rather than only watched on video. Achology Membership is the community subscription; every course purchase includes three months of it.

Who Achology is for

Achology serves self-directed learners: people building coaching, mentoring, or helping practices; professionals adding psychological skill to work they already do; and people studying purely for their own growth. There are no entry requirements. Those pursuing recognition can progress through the Achology certification pathway, a five-level competency development programme from Achologist to Master Achologist. Related questions

Comparing Achology vs university psychology programmes, how does the approach actually differ? Achology and university psychology programmes are built for different purposes. A university degree is a regulated academic qualification: three or more years of study, formal entry requirements, tuition typically upwards of £27,000 for a UK undergraduate programme, and the only route into statutory professions such as clinical psychology. Achology is an applied psychology academy: no entry requirements, courses from $97 to $299, and a curriculum built around practical application, personal development, and community practice rather than academic assessment. Neither replaces the other; which is right depends entirely on what you want the education to do.

What universities offer that Achology does not

Honesty first. A university programme gives you a recognised academic degree, structured research training, and access to regulated career paths: if your goal is to become a clinical psychologist, a chartered psychologist, or an academic researcher, a university degree is not optional, and Achology is not the right route. Achology is not a university, does not award degrees, and its certifications are educational recognition within its own framework rather than statutory qualifications.

What Achology offers that universities typically do not

Achology's differences are real, and they matter for a different kind of learner:

  • Accessibility. No entry requirements, applications, or prerequisites; anyone willing to learn thoughtfully and apply it responsibly can start immediately, at a fraction of a degree's cost. Individual courses run $97 to $299, full school bundles $987 to $1,337, and the Access All Areas Pass, covering all 28 courses, is $2,995.
  • Breadth over specialisation. The curriculum spans seven schools of applied psychology taught as complementary perspectives rather than competing camps, where a degree usually asks you to specialise in one tradition.
  • Application from day one. Teaching centres on using psychological insight in real life and helping work, rather than working through theory and assessment first.
  • Learning in community. Members practise together through daily live events, peer feedback, and mentorship, where much university study is necessarily solitary.

Which should you choose?

Choose a university programme if you need a formal qualification, a statutory career route, or research training. Choose Achology if your goal is practical psychological competence for personal growth, coaching, mentoring, leadership, or responsible helping work, and you want to start now without academic gatekeeping or degree-level cost. Many members hold degrees already and use Achology for the applied layer their academic study never covered; others come with no academic background at all. Both are legitimate starting points here.

How psychology became institutionalised and gatekept is worth answering plainly. It happened gradually, and mostly for understandable reasons. For most of human history the understanding of mind, emotion and conduct lived in philosophy, spiritual traditions and community wisdom, belonging to no profession. Then it became a science, then a profession, then a clinical infrastructure, and each step had a real purpose.

The sequence

  • Late 1800s: psychology becomes a laboratory science inside universities.
  • Early to mid twentieth century: it professionalises, with degrees, licensing and regulatory bodies.
  • Later twentieth century: diagnostic manuals and healthcare systems organise its clinical wing around formally defined conditions.

Each of those moved psychological understanding further inside institutional walls, and none of them intended to.

What the transition genuinely gained

Fairness requires the credit column, and it is substantial.

Scientific psychology produced knowledge tradition alone never could: tested findings about memory, development, behaviour and effective treatment. Professionalisation protected the vulnerable, because licensing and ethics boards exist for the good reason that unaccountable practice on distressed people causes real harm. And the clinical infrastructure, imperfect as it is, treats conditions that once meant untreated suffering.

None of this was elites hoarding wisdom. It was a field growing standards, and the standards work. Any account that skips this part is selling something.

The side effect Achology responds to

The cost came with the packaging rather than the intent.

As psychology's serious forms became degree-gated professions, the everyday understanding at its heart, of yourself, your relationships, communication and helping, came to feel like professional property too. Something ordinary adults consume through experts rather than learn.

That side effect, not the professions themselves, is what this answers: open-entry applied psychology for the non-clinical uses that were never rightly gated, alongside the professions and with clear boundaries toward them.

It is why the pricing is built as it is, and what the side effect has cost is the companion question.

Each session is built around a single case. The host may share it in advance, which tends to produce a richer discussion, or introduce it at the start.

The group then works it through: what is actually going on, where the opportunities and the risks sit, what a response might look like and what it might cost. Real situations do not arrive labelled with the framework that fits them. The skill being built here is the one that decides everything else in practice: reading what is in front of you accurately before choosing a response. A practitioner who knows six models and cannot tell which the moment calls for is holding tools without judgement.

Hearing five other members read the same case differently is the fastest correction available for that, because it shows you what you did not notice.

These groups sit between theory and practice. Skill workshops rehearse techniques and reflective discussions explore principles; case studies ground both in the complexity of a realistic situation.

They suit any member with course learning to apply, and they are a good place to sharpen judgement before coaching in front of observers, where the reading has to happen live and unaided.

Sessions appear in the Upcoming Events calendar; RSVP and join like any other event. Attending earns one Virtual Achologist Led Training Session (VALTS) credit and hosting earns one Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit instead. Afterwards, submit the claim.

So what types of Achology live events actually run here? Achology's community runs 22 live event types in two tiers. Nine are continuing professional development (CPD)-credit events: structured 90-minute sessions that count toward your CPD record, covering skill practice, reflective discussion, case studies, live coaching, tutorials, and the compliance trainings. All appear in the Upcoming Events calendar at community.achology.com.

The CPD-credit events

The nine CPD-credit event types are: the Skill Development Workshop (Hands-On Practice Session), the Principle-Based Reflective Discussion (Group and Meetup), the Case Study-Based Discussion Group (Peer-to-Peer Learning), The Coaching 'HOT Seat' (The LIVE Coaching Experience), the Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback Session, the Achologist-Led Tutorial (ALT Community Training Session), the Achology Code of Ethics Training, the Code of Character & Conduct Training, and the host training for Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS), formally the Group Facilitation + VALTS Host Training. Attending most of these earns one VALTS credit per session; the two conduct trainings keep your compliance status current instead.

The community events

The thirteen community events are lighter in structure and carry no CPD credit in any role. They include the mentorship groups, such as The Wiser Woman Project and the Coaching Excellence + Impact Mentorship Group, informal meet-ups such as Coffee and Conversation, and discussion formats such as the Achology Book Club and Mission Driven Mondays.

VALTS, PALS and CIPS: the credit types behind the events

Three activity types make up the CPD record. VALTS, Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions, are earned by attending the credit-bearing events above. Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) are earned by taking the coaching, facilitation, or hosting role rather than by attending. Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS) are one-to-one coaching sessions delivered to people outside the community, arranged through The Coaching Board rather than the events calendar. Every credit claim is verified by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) committee before it is committed to your record.

So how do you choose the right event for where you are right now? Almost every event welcomes all members, so choosing well is about matching your stage to the format that will stretch you most productively rather than about meeting prerequisites. Start with the conversational formats, move into hands-on practice as confidence grows, and take the evaluated formats when you are ready to have your work reviewed.

If you are new to the community

Begin with the observation-friendly and discussion-led formats: the Principle-Based Reflective Discussion, the mentorship groups, and The Coaching HOT Seat as an observer.

That last one is the most useful thing a new member can do, and the least demanding. You earn a Virtual Achologist Led Training Session (VALTS) credit simply for watching skilled coaching closely, and watching several coaches handle the same person teaches more in ninety minutes than a module does.

If you are building practical skill

Prioritise the Skill Development Workshop for guided practice of specific techniques, and the Case Study-Based Discussion Group for applying frameworks to realistic situations.

Then start delivering one-to-one peer coaching through The Coaching Board, which is where your Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credits begin.

If you are preparing for professional practice

Move toward the evaluated formats: coaching in the HOT Seat, taking the coaching role in a Live Coaching Practice session, and attending Achologist-Led Tutorials.

Hosting is its own step, covered in whether members can host.

The honest rule of thumb

Pick the format that makes you slightly uncomfortable rather than the one you will enjoy.

Members drift toward discussion formats and stay there, because discussing coaching is pleasant and being observed coaching is not. The discomfort is the signal you are at the right event, and it is the same reason the senior levels require the harder formats rather than more of the easy ones.

Nothing stops you attending anything from day one. No enrolment is required, and the recommended pathway sets out the wider sequence.

Because the events are not an extension of the courses, they are the other half of the education.

Course study builds knowledge. Attending is open. Hosting is earned.

So what is the recommended practice pathway inside Achology? It is the member journey through six continuing professional development (CPD) statuses: Achology Member, Certified Achologist, Achologist Adept, Senior Achologist, Senior Achologist (II), and Master Achologist. Each step is earned through a blend of course study and verified practice rather than course completion alone, and the pathway is self-paced: you progress when you meet a level's milestones, not on a timetable. The full per-level requirements live in the Achology CPD Handbook, and progression runs through the Achology certification pathway.

The three activity types that carry you along it

Progress is built from three kinds of verified activity. Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) are earned by attending the continuing professional development (CPD)-credit live events. Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) are earned by taking the coaching, facilitation, or hosting role. Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS) are one-to-one coaching delivered to people outside the community, and they enter the pathway at Senior Achologist (Level One), by which point your course knowledge, community practice, and peer feedback have prepared you for real-world clients. Alongside these sit the compliance trainings, including the Code of Ethics Training, which keeps your ethics status current through annual attendance.

How progress is verified

Nothing self-reported goes straight onto your record. Credit claims are submitted through the member self-report form and independently verified by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) committee, before being committed. That verification is what makes each status mean something: it is evidence of practice done, not attendance logged.

The deliberate design behind it

The pathway is demanding by design. Studying a course gives you information and a framework; practising inside the community, receiving coaching, and eventually coaching others is what turns the framework into genuine skill. Choose events to match your stage, and let the pathway pull you from learning about the work to doing it.

So how do you build real competence with Achology, rather than just becoming informed? By engaging the whole learning ecosystem rather than completing courses alone. Course study builds knowledge; competence is built on top of it through Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS), the live training events you attend; Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS), the sessions where you take the coaching or facilitation role; and, at senior levels, Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS), real coaching delivered to people outside the community. Achology's entire structure rests on the principle that competence develops through doing, receiving feedback, and contributing.

Knowledge first, then practice

A course gives you frameworks and a mental model: valuable, and not the same thing as skill. A practitioner who knows theory but cannot apply it under the pressure of a real conversation is informed, not yet competent. The live events exist to close that gap: skill workshops to rehearse techniques, case-study groups to apply frameworks to realistic situations, and live coaching formats to practise in front of people who tell you honestly what they saw.

Then contribution

The shift from participant to contributor is where skill compounds. Delivering one-to-one peer coaching through The Coaching Board, taking the coaching role in evaluated sessions, hosting events once trained, and eventually coaching people outside the community through Competency Improvement Practice Sessions: each puts you in the practitioner's seat, and each is verified onto your continuing professional development (CPD) record by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) committee.

The measure

Competence at Achology is demonstrated through the breadth and depth of verified practice, not the number of certificates collected. If you want the structured version of this route, the practice pathway lays it out level by level, and the Achology certification pathway is where progression is recognised.

new_seo_title: Achology Certification and Competence: How They Relate
new_seo_description: Achology certification and competence are related but distinct. A certificate confirms course completion; competence is built through verified practice.
new_body_html:
So how do Achology certification and competence actually relate to each other? They are related and deliberately distinct. Completing a Practitioner Certification Course earns a certificate, and that certificate confirms you engaged with the material. It does not, by itself, mean you are ready to practise professionally. Competence is developed separately, through the member journey layered on top of the course study.

Where competence actually accrues

In the practice, and each part does a different job:

  • Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS): live training you take part in rather than watch.
  • Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS): coaching you deliver rather than receive.
  • Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS): real sessions with people outside the community.
  • The ethics and character trainings, which keep the professional and personal strands current.

All of it is independently verified by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) before it counts, which is what makes the record mean anything to somebody outside.

What a certificate does and does not claim

Achology is openly honest about this because the industry often is not.

A certificate of completion marks that a course was finished. It does not qualify you to use regulated titles such as therapist or counsellor, and that boundary does not move. Whether you can practise professionally depends on your actual competence, your ethical grounding and your jurisdiction's regulations rather than on any certificate.

Treating completion as the finish line is the assumption the whole pathway exists to correct, and the two certificates are named differently so that the distinction survives contact with a CV.

Why separate them at all

Because a provider that certified competence on completion would be certifying something it had not seen.

Nobody at Achology watches you finish a video. They do watch you coach, in evaluated sessions with structured feedback, and that is the only evidence worth putting a name to.

It is also the argument against fast certification: a credential that arrives at the end of the watching describes the watching.

So can Achology members host their own events? Yes, and hosting is actively encouraged: facilitating others develops you faster than almost anything else on the pathway. Hosting runs on two tiers. Continuing professional development (CPD)-credit events are open to any member at Achologist level or above who has completed the host training for Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS), formally the Group Facilitation + VALTS Host Training (Learn to Host Events); community events require informal Eldership approval, extended as an invitation when the team recognises a member is ready.

Tier 1: hosting the CPD-credit events

Once you have reached Achologist level and completed the host training, you can host the Skill Development Workshop, the Principle-Based Reflective Discussion, the Case Study-Based Discussion Group, The Coaching 'HOT Seat', the Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback Session, and the two conduct trainings, all without further approval. Two exceptions apply: the Achologist-Led Tutorial requires Achologist Adept level or above, because the host teaches actual content, and the host training itself is delivered exclusively by Eldership members. Hosting a CPD-credit event earns you one Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit per session.

Tier 2: hosting community events

Community events, from the informal meet-ups to the substantial mentorship groups, have no application process. Readiness is developed through sustained participation in The Craft of Facilitation: Learn to Become an Event Host mentorship group and the host training sessions; when the Eldership team sees you are ready, they invite you. The approval is recognition, not a hurdle.

How to publish once qualified

Every event uses a locked template from the Event Descriptions Library in the community: you copy the template, write the one paragraph describing your specific session's theme, upload the event type's image, and publish without changing the locked sections. Be honest with the Eldership team, and yourself, about which formats you are ready for.

new_seo_description: To become a Master Achologist you progress through six CPD statuses: five courses, 50 VALTS, 50 PALS as coach, 50 CIPS, then annual maintenance.
new_body_html:
So how do you become a Master Achologist? By progressing through all six statuses of the continuing professional development (CPD) pathway, from Achology Member through Certified Achologist, Achologist Adept, Senior Achologist and Senior Achologist (II), to Master Achologist, meeting each level's verified requirements in turn. Levels cannot be skipped, the totals are cumulative across the journey, and the pathway is self-paced: it is a long-term professional commitment, not a weekend certification.

What Level 5 requires

The Master Achologist level asks for, cumulatively: five Practitioner Certification Courses, which must include The Skilled Helper Practitioner Course (Advanced to Expert), plus three School of Personal Growth and Development courses; 50 Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) across all six VALT types, attending 30 and hosting or co-hosting 20; 50 Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) delivered as coach, of which 8 must come from the alternative types (the HOT Seat as coach, the Live Coaching Practice session as coach, or the Achologist-Led Tutorial as host); and 30 one-to-one Focused Practice Sessions received as client.

Alongside these sit 50 Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS), real coaching sessions offered to people outside the community, with a maximum of six counting from any one individual, plus the compliance strands: the live Code of Ethics Training annually, and 8 or more of the 10 Code of Character and Conduct virtue sessions current within any rolling 12 months.

The status is maintained, not kept

Master Achologist is not a permanent designation. From 1 January of the first full calendar year after qualifying, annual maintenance applies: hosting a minimum of ten VALTS and eight PALS-as-coach sessions across the named formats, receiving six one-to-one sessions, offering eight CIPS, the annual ethics training, the rolling conduct-code currency.

Where to start

Wherever you are on the pathway, the route is the same: study, practise, contribute, and claim each activity through the self-report form for the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) verification. The practice pathway article gives the level-by-level shape, and the full requirements live in the Achology CPD Handbook.

So can you download Achology course content to watch offline? Partly. The written resources inside your courses, the PDFs, worksheets, templates and reference materials, download freely: save them to your device and keep them permanently. Video lessons stream online only and cannot be downloaded, so watching the teaching itself needs a connection.

What downloads, and how

Wherever a course provides a written resource, a download option sits with it. Click it, save the file, and it is yours for ongoing professional use.

Downloading the materials as you work through a course is worth doing deliberately rather than when you happen to need them, because it builds you a permanent working library alongside the streamed teaching. Members who practise regularly tend to use the worksheets far more than they rewatch the videos. Where to find the resources for your course covers locating them.

Why the videos stream only

Two reasons, and the second is the one that benefits you.

The first is protection of the course material: keeping video on the platform prevents unauthorised distribution, which is the same reason course content cannot be redistributed and why copies found elsewhere are not legitimate.

The second is that you are always watching the current version. Achology updates courses as the curriculum develops, at no extra cost, and those improvements reach you automatically. A downloaded copy would freeze a lesson at the moment you saved it, which quietly undermines the lifetime access that is meant to keep the course useful for years.

Studying when you know you will be offline

The platform is browser-based and works on computers, tablets and phones, so streaming is not tied to a desk. It is tied to connectivity.

If you have a commute, a flight or a patchy connection ahead, the practical approach is to download the written materials for the lessons you plan to cover and save the video watching for when you are connected. The reflective exercises and worksheets are the parts that reward slow, undistracted attention anyway, so offline time is often better spent on them than on watching.

So you cannot log in to Achology community: what is going wrong? Almost every login failure has one of four causes: the wrong email address, an expired or mistyped password, browser cookie problems, or a verification email sitting in spam. Work through the checks below in order. Most people are back in within minutes.

The checks, in order

  • Confirm you are using the exact email address your membership is registered with. A different address, even one of your own, is the single commonest cause.
  • Use "Forgot password" on the login screen at community.achology.com and follow the reset link.
  • Check your spam and junk folders for the reset or verification email.
  • Clear your browser's cookies and cache, then try again.
  • Try a different browser or device, which tells you whether the problem is the account or the machine.

Why these five, and not a longer list

Because of where the community actually runs. It is hosted on Circle, a separate platform from the site you are reading now, and it signs you in by email address rather than a username. That is what makes the first check the commonest fix: people register with one address and later try to sign in with another.

The cookie check matters for the same structural reason. Because sign-in involves a second platform, browsers with strict third-party cookie settings can interrupt it, and Safari on iOS is the known case. A login loop that returns you to the same screen is almost always this rather than a wrong password. Which browsers and devices work best covers the settings.

If none of that works

Contact support with three things ready: the email address you are trying to log in with, your device and browser, and a screenshot of the error you see. That combination usually resolves the remaining cases in one exchange rather than several, and what to include in a support request explains why each part matters.

How to contact support gives the routes. Nothing you have bought is at risk while you are locked out: course access and membership are attached to your account, not to the session, and they are waiting when you get back in.

Tune each type to how you actually use the community

Open your notification settings and work through the three deliberately.

  • Email suits what you want a record of: event reminders, replies to your posts.
  • In-app suits everything you are happy to find next time you visit.
  • Push, through the phone app, suits only what should interrupt you, which for most members is live-event start times and direct messages.

Set each category per type rather than globally and the volume lands where you want it. Managing notifications covers the per-space controls, which are the ones that make the difference.

Two specific cases

If email is switched on but nothing arrives, check spam and junk and search for messages from Circle rather than from Achology, since the platform is the sender. That is the same cause behind missing password reset emails.

If you want push and have never had one, you need the community app installed with notifications permitted in your phone's own settings, which is a separate switch from the one inside the app.

Why this is worth ten minutes

Because of what you would miss. Most of what happens here can be caught up on later, but the live events cannot: they happen at a time, and the practice that your progression depends on happens in them.

Too many alerts and you start ignoring all of them, including the event reminder. Too few and the session you meant to attend runs without you. Neither is a small loss, which is why the settings are worth setting deliberately rather than tolerating.

So you have audio or camera problems in a live session? The usual causes are browser permissions blocking access, the wrong input or output device selected in the session settings, or another application holding your camera. Most cases are fixed in a couple of minutes.

The checks, in order

  • Confirm your browser has permission to use the microphone and camera. The prompt is easy to dismiss without noticing, and once blocked it stays blocked until you change it in the browser's site settings.
  • Open the session's audio and video settings and check the right microphone, speakers and camera are selected, particularly if you use a headset or an external webcam.
  • Close other applications holding the camera or microphone, such as Zoom, Teams or FaceTime. A device held by one app is unavailable to another.
  • Quit the browser completely and rejoin.
  • On a phone, check the community app has microphone and camera permission in your device settings, which is separate from the app's own.

Test before the session, not during it

This is the practical advice worth taking. Joining five minutes early and speaking once to check you can be heard costs nothing, and it is the difference between fixing a permission and missing the part of the session you came for.

It matters more here than in an ordinary meeting because of what these sessions are. In a HOT Seat or a coaching practice session you may be coaching or being coached, and losing audio halfway through is not a technical inconvenience but the end of somebody's session.

If it persists

Try a different browser or device to work out whether the fault is the machine or the account, and check your connection is stable, since live video needs consistent bandwidth rather than raw speed. Chrome and Firefox handle the live features most reliably.

Tell the host in the session chat so they can work around it rather than waiting on you. If it recurs across sessions, contact support with your device and browser details.

So you cannot send or receive messages in the community? The cause is almost always a messaging availability setting, either yours or the other member's, rather than a technical fault. Circle, the community platform, gives every member control over whether they can be messaged directly, and those settings can block messaging in both directions without showing an obvious error.

Check your own setting first

Open your profile or account settings in the community and find your direct messaging availability. If it is switched off, nobody can message you, and in some configurations you cannot start conversations either. Switch it on and test with a member you know.

This is the fix in most cases, and it is easy to have switched off without remembering: the setting sits alongside the notification controls that most members adjust when they first join.

If your setting is on and it still fails

Then the other member has most likely disabled theirs, which is their privacy choice working exactly as intended rather than a fault to report. Arrange contact another way: reply to one of their posts, or speak to them at a live event.

Achology collects the personal data needed to run your account, deliver your courses, process payments, and operate its learning community: contact details, account and registration information, transaction records, communications, technical usage data, and marketing preferences. The categories, in plain terms

The Privacy Notice lists the categories of personal data Achology may collect. Not every category applies to every person.

  • Contact information: your name, postal address, email address, and telephone number.

  • Transaction and service information: courses purchased, events attended, certifications awarded, and credits earned.
  • Communications: emails, support enquiries, and other correspondence with Achology.

  • Technical and usage data: device and browser information collected through cookies, explained in the Cookie Policy.
  • Marketing preferences: your choices about receiving communications.
  • Financial information: payment details, handled securely and in most cases processed by third-party payment providers rather than stored by Achology.

Two further categories apply only in specific situations: recruitment information if you apply for a role, and business or professional information where it is relevant to the services provided.

Special category data is not collected

Achology does not intentionally collect what UK data protection law calls special categories of personal data: health information, racial or ethnic origin, religious or philosophical beliefs, political opinions, trade union membership, genetic or biometric data, or sexual orientation. If you volunteer something of that kind yourself, for example in a community discussion, it is not used for any specific purpose and is handled under the Privacy Notice.

Where this is set out

So do you need qualifications to study at Achology? No. There are no academic prerequisites, no psychology credentials required and no entrance requirements. The curriculum is designed for reflective, self-directed adults aged 18 and over, whatever their formal education. The only ordering requirements anywhere in the catalogue are two advanced practitioner courses that build on their own foundation courses.

What matters instead of credentials

  • Reflectiveness: the willingness to examine your own thinking, behaviour and assumptions honestly rather than defensively.
  • Maturity: the capacity to engage with challenging ideas, tolerate discomfort, and take responsibility for how you apply what you learn.
  • Consistency: applied psychology is practice, and practice rewards showing up.

None of those correlates neatly with degrees, which is exactly why degrees are not required. Who Achology is designed for describes the same character at more length.

Why it works this way

Achology's position is that psychological education should not be gatekept by academic institutions. Understanding human behaviour, developing self-knowledge and learning to help others are capacities adults can build directly, and how the subject came to be gatekept sets out the argument in full.

The Trust Statement describes the learner the environment assumes: an autonomous adult ready to be challenged. That is a real expectation rather than flattery, and why nobody holds your hand through it explains what follows from it.

What no entry requirement does not mean

It does not mean the standard is low, and it is worth separating the two, because they are routinely confused in this industry.

The gate is at the entrance in most education. Here it sits at the other end: progression past the first level requires demonstrated practice, independently verified, which no amount of prior study shortens. Anyone may begin. Nobody is waved through.

What your certificate is, regardless of your background

Educational recognition within Achology's framework. Not a statutory qualification, and nothing about your prior education changes what it is, in either direction. What a certificate proves is the honest account.

new_body_html:
Is there homework in Achology courses, and will you be assessed? Not in the traditional sense. Achology courses use reflective exercises, practice activities and self-assessment prompts rather than graded homework, and nothing is submitted for marking. Certificates of completion are issued for finished courses, and the emphasis throughout is on practical integration rather than academic testing.

What the exercises actually look like

Most courses include guided reflection: identify three situations where you responded defensively and what triggered it; describe a relationship pattern that repeats and the part you play in maintaining it; practise a communication technique in five real conversations and note what happened.

These exist to move the learning into your own life. They serve you rather than a grader, which is also why nobody checks whether you did them, and why the written materials are the half of a course most often skipped and most worth doing.

Why nothing is graded

Because a grade would measure the wrong thing and quietly change what you do.

An assignment written to be marked is written for the marker. It gets tidied, and the parts where you actually struggled get left out, which are precisely the parts the exercise was for. An honest answer to "describe a pattern you maintain" is not something anybody performs well for a score.

It also follows from how Achology treats learners. The teaching assumes capable adults who are here because they want the thing itself, and personal responsibility for your own learning is the stated expectation rather than a slogan.

Where you are actually assessed

There is assessment here, and it is nowhere near the coursework. It happens in the live practice.

When you coach another member while a group observes, or take a coaching role in a live session, you receive structured feedback from senior members, and every claim you make is independently verified before it counts. That is a far harder test than an essay, and it is what separates completing a course from being competent.

So the honest summary is that the courses are not assessed and the practitioner is. The two certificates record exactly that difference.

new_seo_description: Achology's approach to open discussion favours exploring perspectives with curiosity over debating to win. Differing views are expected and welcomed.
new_body_html:
Achology's approach to open discussion values reflective conversation over adversarial debate. The aim is to understand a different worldview and come away with a more nuanced one, not to prove a position right and the rest wrong. Differing views are expected and welcomed, and the Trust Statement sets the standard: engage critically rather than defensively, reflect before reacting.

Why the community works this way

Because of what is being taught. The ideas here are frameworks for understanding people, open to interpretation, and they land differently depending on somebody's experience, values and temperament.

Treating discussion as a contest closes down exactly the perspective-taking that applied psychology trains. Working out why somebody sees a thing differently teaches more than winning an exchange with them, and it is the same skill you will need in the chair opposite a client who does not see their situation the way you do.

It also follows from the curriculum's own shape. Achology teaches several traditions without ranking them, so a community that insisted on one right answer would be contradicting the syllabus.

What that looks like in practice

  • Ask what an idea looks like from the other person's position before arguing with it.
  • Offer your own view as a perspective rather than a verdict.
  • Let a discussion end with two understood positions rather than one declared winner.

Disagreeing is fine and often useful. The culture asks only that it is done to understand rather than to defeat, which is why the way you ask a question decides most of what you get back.

Being challenged is the product, not a fault in it

Course content may unsettle beliefs you hold, and members will sometimes say things you disagree with strongly. That is part of the education rather than a failure of it, and what to do when the material challenges you takes it seriously.

The people who get least from this place are usually the ones who came for confirmation, which is the same point made in who Achology is not designed for.

Where the boundaries sit

Open discussion runs inside the Community Code of Conduct and the moderation standards. Respect is not optional; certainty is. If a discussion stops feeling safe rather than merely uncomfortable, that has its own route, and the distinction between the two is worth holding.

The Achology peer learning culture runs on a simple idea: you learn psychology by practising it with other people rather than by studying alone. Members practise, discuss and refine skills together through live sessions, peer practice and mentorship groups. The culture expects maturity, honest feedback and shared responsibility, and everybody participates as both learner and contributor.

What shapes the culture

The Code of Character and Conduct sets the tone: nine virtues drawn from Aristotle, trained across the community rather than treated as an academic exercise.

Alongside it sits the Community Code of Conduct as the behavioural standard, and the Trust Statement describing the relationship the whole environment rests on: autonomous adults, engaging thoughtfully, taking responsibility for themselves.

How the learning actually works

Skills taught in the courses get rehearsed with real people in structured formats: live training, peer coaching, and mentorship groups.

Honest feedback is normal rather than tiptoed around, because feedback is where development happens. Members span every level from newcomers to Master Achologists, which produces natural mentoring: people further along practise their craft by helping people earlier in it, and their progression depends on doing so.

The thing that surprises new members

How ordinary it is, and how little performance there is in it.

A community about psychology could easily become a place where people demonstrate insight at each other. This one mostly does not, because the formats keep putting members in positions where they are visibly not yet good: coaching somebody while a group watches, examining a virtue they fall short on, asking a question that reveals what they have not understood.

Being seen mid-learning is the normal state here rather than an embarrassment, and that is what makes asking a genuinely specific question possible.

What it asks of you

Participation rather than attendance. Posting, replying, turning up to sessions, and eventually offering something back. Members who only read tend to finish courses; members who take part tend to change how they practise.

Where disagreement arises, it is engaged rather than avoided, and there is a route if something stops feeling safe rather than merely uncomfortable.

To ask a question in Achology and get a useful answer back, the quality of what you receive tracks the quality of what you ask. Be specific, show your own thinking first, give enough context for people to place you, and post in the space where the right members will see it. Questions asked that way draw detailed responses. Vague ones draw silence.

Be specific

"Can anyone help me with Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)?" sits unanswered because nobody knows what help you need.

Compare: "I am working through the rapport-building module in the NLP Practitioner course and I am struggling with the difference between matching and mirroring in a professional conversation. How do other members apply the distinction in practice?"

The second tells the community what you are stuck on, where you are in the material, and what kind of answer would help. It is also three times as likely to get a reply from somebody who has hit the same wall.

Show your thinking first

A question that includes your current understanding, "here is how I read it, and here is where it stops making sense", invites members to engage with your reasoning rather than lecture from scratch.

It also signals you have done your part, which is the shared responsibility the community runs on.

Why vagueness is usually protection

Worth naming, because it is rarely laziness.

A general question keeps the discussion on a topic rather than on your work, and nobody discovers what you have not grasped. That instinct is understandable and it costs you the answer, since a question that reveals nothing gives nobody anything to respond to.

Being seen mid-learning is the normal state here, not an embarrassment. The members who get most from this place are the ones asking the questions they were slightly reluctant to type.

Keep the conversation going

Post in the relevant space so the right people see it, ask open questions rather than yes-or-no ones, and reply to the replies. A short exchange nearly always produces a better answer than a single response, and a disagreement handled well produces the best answers of all.

The Achology community moderation rules centre on the Community Code of Conduct, named in the Terms and Conditions as part of your agreement. The Terms also state that access can be withdrawn for breaching it, immediately where a breach is serious or repeated. Around that standard sit five shared principles and a virtues-based character framework.

The enforceable standard

The Community Code of Conduct is delivered as a short video course and sets what every member agrees to in the community's spaces.

Moderation upholds it: community managers act on breaches, and sustained failure puts membership at risk, which the suspension article sets out in full. That is the hard edge, and it exists so the softer culture can work rather than instead of it.

The five shared principles

Respect and inclusivity, active engagement, integrity and professionalism, ethical conduct, and shared responsibility.

The last matters most in practice. Maintaining the community's standards is treated as every member's job rather than only the moderators', which is why the culture holds at scale. A community policed only from above develops the habit of reporting; one where members address a souring thread themselves develops something better.

The character framework behind it

The Code of Character and Conduct approaches conduct from the other direction: nine virtues, drawn from Aristotle, taught as a practical framework rather than an academic one.

Rules police behaviour. Virtues develop the person. Achology runs both deliberately, because rules alone produce members who stay just inside them, and that is not the same as a community worth being in.

What the rules are protecting

Worth naming, because a conduct standard can read as bureaucratic until you see what depends on it.

Members bring genuine difficulties to live coaching sessions, practise badly in front of each other, and examine their own character honestly in groups. None of that survives in a space where conduct is unreliable, and the loss would be silent: people simply become careful.

What the culture feels like day to day describes the result, how disagreement is handled covers the hardest case, and what to do when something crosses a line is the route.

new_seo_description: If an Achology discussion feels unsafe, speak up, step away, or report it to the host or support@achology.com. You are never alone.
new_body_html:
If an Achology discussion feels unsafe, take your own judgement seriously and act: in a live event you can speak up, alert the host, or simply leave the session; in a discussion space you can report the post or contact a community manager; and for anything serious, contact Achology directly at support@achology.com or through the contact form. You are not expected to resolve a harmful situation alone, and sustained failure to uphold community standards puts a member's access at risk under the Terms and Conditions.

Recognising when a line has been crossed

Applied psychology discussions sometimes touch difficult and personal territory, and most of the time that is where the richest learning happens. A boundary issue is different: unsolicited quasi-therapeutic advice, disclosure that pressures others to match it, disrespectful behaviour, or an atmosphere that has genuinely stopped feeling safe to learn in. If something feels wrong, treat that response as information rather than dismissing it.

The three responses, matched to the moment

In the moment, in a live session: name the discomfort if you are able ("I'd like to step back from this"), signal the host privately, or leave; leaving a session needs no justification. Afterwards, or in written spaces: report the post or message a community manager, who moderate against the Community Code of Conduct. For anything serious or unresolved: bring it to Achology at support@achology.com with what happened and where, so it can be handled properly.

Where responsibility sits

Achology moderates its spaces to uphold respect and integrity, and it also does not supervise peer interactions or verify members' competence, so your own boundaries and choices remain yours, as the Disclaimers set out. The two halves work together: the community holds the standard, and you hold your line. They differ in what they treat as the lever of change: thought patterns, language, awareness, the person's own growth tendency, goals, wellbeing, or everyday effectiveness. All seven are introduced on the Academy schools page.

The seven, and what each treats as the lever

  • The School of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP): how language and subjective experience shape behaviour, and how changing the patterns changes the result.
  • The School of Cognitive Behavioural Psychology (CBP): the relationship between thoughts, feelings, and behaviour, and the structured restructuring of unhelpful patterns.
  • The School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping: frameworks for helping others move from where they are to where they want to be, including the structured helping models used in professional practice.
  • The School of Person-Centred Counselling and Psychology: the tradition built on human autonomy and the person's own tendency toward growth, where the helper's stance matters as much as any technique.
  • The School of Mindfulness, Applied Insight and Wisdom (MIW): present-moment awareness, acceptance, and the applied use of attention.
  • The School of Mental Health, Wellness and Emotional Resilience: psychological wellbeing, resilience, and the understanding that supports both.
  • The School of Personal Growth and Development (PGD): practical effectiveness in living, from communication and confidence to discipline and purpose.

How the differences help you choose

The schools are not levels; they are lenses, and none is a prerequisite for another. Choose by the question you most want answered: change how you think (CBP), change how you communicate and perceive (NLP), help others professionally (Life Coaching or Person-Centred), steady the mind (MIW), understand wellbeing (Mental Health), or sharpen everyday living (PGD). Many learners eventually study across several traditions, which is what the integrated curriculum is built for; the basic map of the schools is in What are the seven schools of Achology?

post_title: What are the six Achology CPD member levels?
old_keyword: what are the six Achology CPD member levels
new_seo_title: The Six Achology CPD Member Levels, In Order|Achology Help
new_seo_description: The six Achology CPD member levels run from Achology Member to Master Achologist. Here is the full ladder and how you move up.
new_body_html:
The six Achology CPD member levels are, in order: Achology Member, Achologist, Achologist Adept, Senior Achologist (Level One), Senior Achologist (Level Two), and Master Achologist. CPD means continuing professional development, the record of practice and learning you build over time. Six levels means five steps up, and every one of them is earned through practice that somebody else has checked, not through time served, fees paid, or a course finished and filed away.

What each level means

  • Achology Member: the starting point, where learning stops being something you watch and becomes something you take part in.
  • Achologist: foundational competence in practice, ethics, and self-awareness. This is the first verified level.
  • Achologist Adept: the turning point. You begin coaching others and hosting sessions, rather than only receiving them.
  • Senior Achologist (Levels One and Two): theory, practice, and leadership brought together, and the stage at which you start coaching people from outside the community.
  • Master Achologist: the highest level, reached through mastery, mentorship, and contribution to other members' development.

What the first year actually looks like

The pathway can read as a wall of requirements, so it helps to see the first step on its own. To move from Member to Achologist, you complete one Practitioner Certification course, attend six Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) , the community's live group training, across at least two different types, and receive six Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) , one-to-one coaching delivered to you by another member. Notice that nothing on that first list asks you to coach anyone. That is deliberate: before you sit opposite someone who has brought you a real problem, the design wants you to have been that person six times over.

From Achologist Adept onward the direction reverses and you start delivering: coaching other members, co-hosting, then hosting your own sessions. At Senior Achologist (Level One), a third kind of activity begins, Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS) , complimentary coaching offered to people outside Achology, which is the closest the pathway comes to real professional practice.

How you move between levels

Each level has a cumulative checklist, meaning everything earned at earlier levels carries forward. It draws on Practitioner Certification courses, VALTS attended, PALS delivered and received, and, from Senior Achologist (Level One), CIPS, alongside annual Code of Ethics training and Code of Character and Conduct compliance. Every claim is checked by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP), an independent body, before it counts.

Why the levels matter, and one to know early

A verified level is not a badge for its own sake. It is what lets someone outside Achology, a prospective client, an employer, another member choosing a mentor, rely on your standing without having to take your word for it. That is the whole reason the checks exist. It is also why Master Achologist is the one level that is not permanent: it has to be renewed each year, so that the highest standing in the community always describes someone still doing the work, not someone who once did.

If the full pathway looks daunting from where you are standing, nobody meets all six Achology CPD member levels at once. Most members are working on one level at a time, and the first step asks considerably less than the whole list suggests.

post_title: What does it mean to be an Achologist Adept?
old_keyword: what does it mean to be an Achologist Adept
new_seo_title: What It Takes to Become an Achologist Adept|Achology Help
new_seo_description: To become an Achologist Adept is the third member level on Achology's CPD pathway, where you start coaching and hosting.
new_body_html:
To become an Achologist Adept means reaching the third member level, one step above Achologist, and it is where the direction of everything reverses. Until now you have been receiving: coached by others, taught by others, sitting in sessions someone else runs. At Adept, you start delivering.

What you need to reach it

These totals are cumulative, including everything already earned:

  • 2 Practitioner Certification courses in total.
  • 12 Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) in total: attend 8, and co-host or host 4, across at least 2 session types.
  • 12 Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) received as a client.
  • 6 PALS delivered as a coach.
  • The live Code of Ethics training completed within the past 12 months. This annual requirement starts here.
  • All 10 Code of Character and Conduct sessions completed, then 8 of the 10 kept current.

What actually changes

Three things begin at Adept that were not asked of you before.

You coach another member for the first time, as the practitioner rather than the client. You move from co-hosting into hosting your own sessions. And the annual ethics training becomes a permanent fixture at every level above this one.

That yearly return to the Code of Ethics is not box-ticking. It is what lets you tell a client, honestly, that you have thought about ethical practice recently, rather than once, years ago, before you had ever sat with a real person.

On the first coaching session

Most people find the first one the hard part, and that is entirely normal.

Worth remembering: by the time you reach Adept you will have received twelve coaching sessions yourself. You have seen it done twelve times, from the seat of the person it was done for.

That is the design, not a coincidence. It is also why the character strand matters more from here: holding 8 of your 10 Code of Character and Conduct sessions current is what keeps your standing, so the step up from Achologist is as much about staying engaged as ticking activities off.

post_title: What is a Senior Achologist, and what are the two levels?
old_keyword: what is a Senior Achologist, and what are the two levels
new_seo_title: The Two Senior Achologist Levels, Explained|Achology Help
new_seo_description: The two Senior Achologist levels are the advanced stage of Achology's CPD pathway: Senior Achologist I and II, and what each requires.
new_body_html:
The two Senior Achologist levels sit in the advanced stage of Achology's pathway, past Achologist Adept. The difference between them is roughly the difference between practising well and being able to develop other people.

Senior Achologist (Level One)

This is where coaching people outside Achology begins. These totals are cumulative, including everything already earned:

  • 3 Practitioner Certification courses (total), including Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP).
  • 1 course from the School of Personal Growth and Development.
  • 24 Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS), with all 6 session types covered.
  • 18 Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) received as a client.
  • 12 PALS delivered as a coach, at least one of them a Live Coaching Practice session, in front of observers who give feedback.
  • 10 Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS).
  • Code of Ethics training and Code of Character and Conduct compliance current.

The real change here is the CIPS: complimentary coaching offered to people outside the community. Coaching a fellow member is one thing; they understand the learning context and forgive the rough edges.

Coaching someone from outside, who simply wants help, is another thing entirely. It is the step from practising in a safe room to doing the actual work, which is why it waits until this level.

The Live Coaching Practice requirement is the quieter marker of the same shift. Public practice starts at Senior Achologist (Level One), and becomes the theme of Senior Achologist (Level Two).

Senior Achologist (Level Two)

This level is about advanced facilitation and coaching in public. The numbers grow, but the meaningful shift is in the kind of coaching required:

  • 36 VALTS in total.
  • 24 PALS received as a client.
  • 24 PALS delivered as a coach, 8 of them from the harder formats.
  • 24 CIPS.

Those harder formats are coaching while a group observes, coaching in a live HOT Seat, or hosting a tutorial. They are the formats that put your practice in front of feedback, which is how it sharpens.

Both levels are cumulative, so nothing resets. Above Senior Achologist (Level Two) sits Master Achologist, and every claim along the way is verified by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) before it counts.

post_title: How can I advance from Achology Member to Achologist?

Advancing from Achology Member to Achologist takes three things: complete one Practitioner Certification course, attend six live group training sessions, and receive six one-to-one coaching sessions as a client. Once the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) has checked each one, you are an Achologist, the second of the six member levels.

The first step in full

  • 1 Practitioner Certification course completed.
  • 6 Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) attended, across at least 2 session types.
  • 6 Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) received as a client: one-to-one coaching delivered to you by another member.

How long it tends to take

There is no fixed clock on this. The courses are self-paced, and the six sessions and six coaching slots happen at the rhythm of the live calendar, so most people measure this step in months rather than weeks, fitted around the rest of life.

A realistic first month is less about racing the checklist and more about finding your feet: working through a course, sitting in on a few sessions, and receiving your first coaching as a client.

The annual Code of Ethics training is not required for this step; it begins at Achologist Adept. You will need all ten Code of Character and Conduct sessions before progressing past Achologist, so many members quietly work through those during this stage rather than facing them all later.

Why you receive before you deliver

Notice that nothing on this list asks you to coach anyone. That is deliberate, and it may be the most considered decision in the whole pathway.

Before you sit opposite someone who has brought you a real problem, the design wants you to have been that person six times over: to know what it feels like when a coach rushes you, or fills a silence you needed. You learn that from the other chair, not from a module.

If you are not yet a member, the free membership tier lets you apply for coaching and attend free events, which is where most people start.

post_title: What are my requirements to maintain Master Achologist status?
old_keyword: what are my requirements to maintain Master Achologist status
new_seo_title: How to Maintain Master Achologist Status|Achology Help
new_seo_description: To maintain Master Achologist status, you renew it yearly: hosting, coaching, CIPS, and compliance requirements set out here.
new_body_html:
To maintain Master Achologist status each year, you complete a set of annual requirements; the title is not kept by having earned it once. Every calendar year, from 1 January of your first full year after qualifying, you complete a set of annual requirements. Miss them and the status lapses until you restore it.

What each year asks

  • 10 Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) hosted: two each of the five host-eligible types.
  • 8 Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) delivered as a coach, spread across the coaching and tutorial formats.
  • 6 PALS received as a client.
  • At least 8 Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS): complimentary coaching offered to people outside Achology.
  • Code of Ethics annual training completed, and the Code of Character and Conduct sessions kept at 8 of 10 current.

What a maintenance year actually looks like

Read that list again and notice what it describes: someone hosting regularly, coaching others, still being coached themselves, and working with people outside the community.

In other words, it is not a set of hoops. It is a picture of a practitioner still fully in the practice, which is exactly what the title is meant to signify.

Why it has to be renewed

Because the alternative makes the title dishonest. If Master Achologist were permanent, it would eventually describe people who reached a standard once, years ago, and have not practised since.

Anyone relying on that standing, a client, an employer, another member choosing a mentor, would be relying on history rather than anything current. The annual requirements keep the meaning attached to the person.

They are also lighter than the full pathway that got you here, because they are a yearly rhythm rather than a climb: host a little, coach a little, keep your compliance current, and the status holds.

If you fall short

The status lapses and is restored once the requirements are met again. Nothing you achieved is erased. Every activity is verified by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) before it counts, the same as at every other level.

post_title: What are VALTS learning sessions within Achology?
old_keyword: what are VALTS learning sessions within Achology
new_seo_title: VALTS Learning Sessions at Achology
new_seo_description: VALTS learning sessions are Achology's 90-minute live group sessions where members practise skills and earn credit toward the next level.
new_body_html:
So what are VALTS learning sessions at Achology? Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) are Achology's live group training sessions: 90-minute events, led by senior members of the community, where you practise applied psychology rather than only watch it explained. They are the backbone of community learning, and attending them is how you earn VALTS credit toward your next member level.

What a session is actually like

A VALTS session is built to be taken part in, not sat through. You join a small group live, work through a skill or an idea with other members, and get observation and feedback in real time. The point is that a technique from a course only becomes yours once you have tried it on a real person and heard honestly how it landed. That is something no recorded lecture can give you, and it is why the sessions are capped in length and kept practical.

The six types

There are six VALT types, each developing a different muscle:

  • Skill Development Workshop: practise a specific skill from a course with a partner or small group, with feedback from the host.
  • Principle-Based Reflective Discussion: work a single principle through a set of questions and apply it to your own life.
  • Case Study-Based Discussion Group: analyse real or hypothetical coaching scenarios as a group.
  • The Coaching HOT Seat: one member takes a live challenge while up to three Achologists coach them and others observe.
  • Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback: an Achologist coaches a member, then receives structured feedback from senior members.
  • Achologist-Led Tutorial: a member teaches a topic from a course to the group, then receives feedback on their delivery.

Why live, and not just video

Achology's whole learning model rests on a simple conviction: information is easy to gather, but competence is only built through practice, in company, with feedback. A practitioner who knows the theory but cannot apply it in a live conversation is informed, not yet skilled. VALTS learning sessions are where that gap is closed, which is why the pathway requires them rather than treating them as optional extras.

How they fit the wider pathway

Attending a VALTS session earns you 1 VALTS credit. Once you reach the right level and complete the host training, hosting one earns you a Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit instead, because you have moved from receiving to delivering. Early on, the requirement is modest: six VALTS across at least two types to reach Achologist. Every session you attend is verified by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) before it counts, and once you are ready, you can host your own.

post_title: What are PALS in Achology, and how can I earn them?
old_keyword: what are PALS in Achology, and how can I earn them
new_seo_title: How to Earn a PALS Credit at Achology
new_seo_description: A PALS credit is earned by coaching or hosting, not by attending. Here is how members earn Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session credit.
new_body_html:
So how do you start earning credit for coaching you deliver, rather than receive? Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Sessions (PALS) are the point where you stop receiving and start contributing. You earn a PALS credit by taking the coaching or facilitation role in a session, never by attending one: the credit goes to the practitioner delivering the work, not the participant. This is what separates PALS from Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) , which you earn by turning up and taking part.

The four ways to earn them

There are four PALS types, and most members earn the bulk of their credits through the first:

  • One-to-one Focused Coaching Practice: a coaching session you deliver to another member, arranged through the Coaching Board in the community. This is the main route.
  • The Coaching HOT Seat, as coach: taking a coaching role during a live HOT Seat event, in front of others, in real time.
  • Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback, as coach: coaching a member while a group observes and then gives feedback on the work.
  • Achologist-Led Tutorial, as host: teaching a topic from a course to a group of peers.

The last three are more demanding than the first, which is deliberate. From Senior Achologist (Level Two) onward, eight of your delivered PALS must come from those alternative types, because each one builds a different edge: coaching under observation, coaching in public, and teaching. Hosting any VALTS session also earns you a PALS credit, once you are qualified to host.

Why you receive before you deliver

There is a reason the pathway has you receive coaching as a client before it asks you to deliver any. By the time you coach another member, you will have sat in the other chair yourself and felt what good and clumsy coaching are like from the inside. That is not something a module can teach you. It is why the first member level asks for PALS received, and coaching delivered only begins at Achologist Adept.

How they add up

Every PALS credit, delivered or received, is verified by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) before it counts toward your next level. The numbers grow as you climb, but they are cumulative and made up of the ordinary work of community life: coaching, being coached, and eventually teaching. Nobody sits down to complete them all at once; they accumulate as you take part.

post_title: What are CIPS in Achology, and when should I obtain them?
old_keyword: what are CIPS in Achology, and when should I obtain them
new_seo_title: What Is a CIPS Credit, and When Is It Needed?
new_seo_description: A CIPS credit is earned by offering free coaching to someone outside Achology. It is first required at Senior Achologist (Level One).
new_body_html:
So when do you start coaching people outside Achology, and what counts? Competency Improvement Practice Sessions (CIPS) are the closest the pathway comes to genuine professional practice. A CIPS credit is earned by offering a complimentary one-to-one coaching session to someone outside the Achology community: a real person, with a real challenge or goal, who simply wants help. You do not need any until Senior Achologist (Level One), and there is a good reason for that timing.

What makes CIPS different

Coaching another member is valuable, but a fellow member understands the learning context, forgives the rough edges, and knows what you are trying to practise. Someone outside the community does none of that. They are not there to help you learn; they are there because they want support. That difference is the whole point. It is the step from practising in a safe room to doing the actual work, and it is the single most formative activity in the pathway precisely because it is the most demanding.

How you arrange them

CIPS are not scheduled calendar events like Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS). They are arranged through the Get Free Coaching board, where people outside Achology browse and apply for sessions that members have offered. post_title: What is the Achology Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC)?

It is the character strand of the continuing professional development (CPD) pathway, trained and tracked alongside the ethics strand.

How it is built

The CCaC runs as ten live sessions: an introduction, then one session for each of the nine virtues, which are Courage, Temperance, Justice, Wisdom, Magnificence, Magnanimity, Friendliness, Truthfulness, and Wittiness. It rests on Aristotle's virtue ethics: the idea that character is not something you are born with, but something developed through deliberate practice, and that each virtue is a balanced middle point between two extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency.

What a virtue session is actually like

A CCaC session is not a lecture on being good. Each virtue is worked through with a set of reflection questions, so the session is really an honest examination of where you sit on that virtue's spectrum. Courage, for example, is the point between recklessness and cowardice, and the session asks you to look at which way you tend to lean, in the company of other members doing the same. That shared honesty is the method: character, in this view, is built by examining it openly, over time, with people who will be straight with you.

Where it sits on the pathway, and why

You complete all ten sessions before you move from Achologist to Achologist Adept, then keep eight of the ten current within any rolling 12-month period. Achology's CCaC is one of three separate codes: distinct from the Code of Ethics, which governs professional practice, and the Community Code of Conduct, which governs behaviour on the community platform. It exists because most training develops only what you can do. The CCaC is how Achology also attends to who you are becoming while you learn, on the plain view that a capable practitioner with poor character helps no one.

The nine, and the extremes each one sits between

The virtues come from Aristotle's virtue ethics, where a virtue is not the opposite of a vice but the balanced middle point between two of them, one of excess and one of deficiency. Read that way the list stops being abstract:

A session is not a lecture on being good. Each virtue is worked through with a set of reflection questions, so the ninety minutes is really an honest examination of where you sit on that virtue's spectrum, in the company of other members doing the same thing.

The middle-point idea is what makes that examination possible. Asked whether you are courageous, most people have no useful answer. Asked which way you tend to lean, toward acting too fast or not acting at all, most people know immediately.

Why character is trained rather than assumed

The nine virtues are treated as qualities developed through practice, not traits you either have or lack. That is the whole reason they are taught in recurring live sessions rather than written into a document members are asked to agree to.

All ten are completed before you progress from Achologist to Achologist Adept. After that you keep 8 of the 10 current within any rolling 12-month period.

What one of these sessions is

A CCaC session is not a lecture on being good. Each virtue is worked through with a set of reflection questions, so the session is really an honest examination of where you actually sit on that virtue, in the company of other members doing the same. Courage, for instance, is treated as the point between recklessness and cowardice, and the session asks which way you tend to lean.

The sessions run regularly through the year, and they are one of the many kinds of live event that are open every week to every member of Achology, alongside the training and coaching formats that the live events article sets out in full.

What "keeping them current" means

Keeping 8 of your 10 CCaC sessions current is an ongoing requirement rather than a hurdle you clear once. Because compliance is measured across a rolling twelve months, sessions gradually drop out of the window as time passes, so staying compliant takes steady engagement rather than a single burst of attendance. Leaving too long a gap is where members find themselves falling short without having decided to.

Holding 8 of your 10 CCaC sessions current is what keeps your status at green. Falling below eight turns it red, which pauses progression until it is restored, though nothing already earned is lost.

Why character is trained at all

This is the part that explains the rest. Most professional training develops only what you can do. The CCaC exists because Achology also attends to who you are becoming while you learn, on the plain view that a capable practitioner with poor character helps nobody.

That is also why it repeats rather than completing. Character, in this account, is not knowledge you acquire once. It is built by examining yourself honestly, over time, with people who will be straight with you, which is exactly what a rolling requirement protects and a one-off course could not.

Where it sits alongside everything else

The CCaC is the character strand of the pathway. Its counterpart is the professional strand, kept current through annual Code of Ethics training, and the two together are the ongoing compliance requirements at every level from Achologist Adept upward.

It is also one of three separate codes, which are easy to confuse: the Code of Ethics governs professional practice, the CCaC develops character, and the Community Code of Conduct governs behaviour on the community platform.
