Green means at least 8 of your 10 Code of Character and Conduct sessions are current within a rolling 12-month period. Red means fewer than 8 are, and while you are red your progression on the pathway is paused until you restore it.

How you move between the two

Compliance is measured across a rolling twelve months rather than a fixed year, so sessions drop out of the window as time passes. Attend nothing for long enough and your count falls below eight on its own, without any decision having been made.

Coming back is the same mechanism in reverse. Attend enough sessions to bring the current count to eight or more and the status returns to green. There is no penalty period and no reapplication.

What red actually stops, and what it does not

Red pauses progression. It does not remove anything you have already earned, and it does not affect your access to courses, events or the community. Every credit and every level already verified stays exactly where it is.

What it means in practice is that further progress waits. Green status is a condition of advancing at every level from Achologist Adept upward, sitting alongside annual Code of Ethics training as the two ongoing compliance requirements.

Why the status exists at all

A status that can lapse is doing something a one-off certificate cannot. The colour is simply the visible form of that distinction. It keeps the character strand of the pathway a live commitment rather than something completed once and filed, which is the same reasoning behind the ethics training repeating annually and behind Master Achologist status having to be renewed each year.

Keeping it green without thinking about it

The sessions run regularly through the year and are one of the many kinds of live event open every week to every member of Achology. post_title: Why does Achology's character code draw from Aristotle?
old_keyword: why does Achology's character code draw from Aristotle
new_seo_title: Achology's Character Code Based on Aristotle
new_seo_description: Achology's character code based on Aristotle treats character as something built through deliberate practice, not something fixed at birth.
new_body_html:
So why is Achology's character code based on Aristotle? Because that tradition treats character as something you develop rather than something you are simply born with or without. For a learning community whose whole premise is that people are capable of growth, a framework built on deliberate practice is the natural fit, and it is what the Code of Character and Conduct rests on.

What virtue ethics actually says

If the phrase is new to you, the idea behind it is plainer than it sounds. Most ethical systems ask what the rules are and whether you followed them. Virtue ethics asks a different question: what kind of person are you becoming.

Its answer is that good character is grown, through practice and honest effort, the same way any skill is. You are not born courageous or patient. You become so by acting that way, repeatedly, until it holds when it is inconvenient.

The idea of the middle point

Aristotle's particular contribution is that a virtue is not the opposite of a vice but the balanced point between two of them, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage sits between recklessness and cowardice; generosity between wastefulness and meanness.

That structure is what makes the nine virtues usable in a session. Asked whether you are courageous, most people have no honest answer available. Asked which way you tend to lean, toward acting too fast or not acting at all, most people know immediately, and can say so in front of others without either boasting or confessing.

Why a rules-based code would not have worked

This is the part that explains the choice rather than merely describing it. Achology already has a rules-based instrument: the Code of Ethics governs professional conduct, and rules are exactly right for that job.

What rules cannot do is prepare somebody for the situations a helping practitioner actually meets, which are rarely covered by a clause. A rule tells you not to breach confidentiality. It does not tell you what to do when a client's difficulty exceeds your competence and they are asking you not to send them elsewhere. What settles that is the character of the person in the chair.

How it runs in practice

Each of the nine virtues is worked through in its own live session, with reflection questions rather than instruction, in the company of other members doing the same. Holding eight of the ten sessions current is what keeps your status green.

The recurring requirement is the philosophy applied to the timetable. If character is built by practice over time, a code you read once could never deliver it, which is why the Code of Character and Conduct repeats and why it is one of three separate codes rather than a section inside the ethics one.

post_title: What are the five principles of Achology's community?
old_keyword: what are the five principles of Achology's community
new_seo_title: The Five Principles of Achology's Community
new_seo_description: The five principles are Respect and Inclusivity, Active Engagement, Integrity and Professionalism, Ethical Conduct, and Shared Responsibility.
new_body_html:
So what are the five principles you agree to as a member of Achology? Respect and Inclusivity, Active Engagement, Integrity and Professionalism, Ethical Conduct, and Shared Responsibility. They come from the Code of Character and Conduct and set the behavioural benchmark for how members treat one another and the space they share.

What each one means

  • Respect and Inclusivity: diversity enriches the community, every perspective is valued, and respect is treated as the basis of growth.
  • Active Engagement: learning is a shared effort, so members take part, listen with intention, ask thoughtful questions and give constructive feedback.
  • Integrity and Professionalism: trust is built through consistent honesty, accountability and professionalism, including upholding confidentiality.
  • Ethical Conduct: members respect others' rights, follow applicable laws, and contribute in ways aligned with the community's standards.
  • Shared Responsibility: the community is a collective effort, so issues are addressed collaboratively rather than left to sour.

What they look like on an ordinary day

These stop being abstractions the moment you are inside the community. Active Engagement is the member who reads a coaching post properly and gives a considered reply rather than a one-line reaction. Shared Responsibility is a group addressing a difficult thread openly and kindly instead of letting it fester. Integrity is somebody holding a confidence they were trusted with, months after the conversation.

None of that is dramatic. The principles describe the ordinary conduct that keeps a large learning community worth being part of, and the peer-learning culture is what they produce when they hold.

Why a learning community needs them stated

Because of what members are asked to do here. People practise coaching on each other, bring real difficulties to live sessions in front of a group, and receive honest feedback on work they are not yet good at.

None of that is possible without a floor under it. A member will not put a genuine problem into a room that might mock it, and will not take feedback from people who have not shown good faith. The five principles are the conditions the practice depends on, which is why they are written down rather than assumed, and why moderation exists to hold them.

They also govern disagreement rather than preventing it: how Achology approaches open disagreement covers that, and what to do if a discussion feels unsafe covers the case where the floor gives way.

How they sit alongside everything else

The five principles are part of the Code of Character and Conduct and work with the nine virtues it trains: the virtues describe the character to develop, the principles describe how to conduct yourself with others while you develop it.

They are the community-facing expression of the ten value commitments and the nine value-based principles, and they are distinct from the Community Code of Conduct, which is the platform's rulebook rather than a development framework.

post_title: What are the suggested character traits of an Achologist?
old_keyword: what are the suggested character traits of an Achologist
new_seo_title: What Character Traits Define an Achologist?
new_seo_description: The Achology Code of Ethics names 22 character traits that define an Achologist, grounded in honesty, integrity, kindness, and empathy.
new_body_html:
So what kind of person is an Achologist expected to be? The Achology Code of Ethics names 22 character traits as the essential personal and moral qualities of an Achologist. They rest on a smaller set of moral foundations, which are honesty, integrity, kindness, fairness, respect, responsibility and empathy, with trust treated as the basis of every professional relationship.

The 22 traits in full

  • Alertness, Attentiveness, Availability, Cautiousness.
  • Compassion, Cooperation, Courage, Diligence.
  • Discipline, Empathy, Enthusiasm, Flexibility.
  • Generosity, Honesty, Humility, Initiative.
  • Integrity, Orderliness, Patience, Positivity.
  • Resilience, Wisdom.

How the list is meant to be used

These 22 character traits are an aspirational inventory rather than a test. They are qualities to grow toward and to examine honestly in yourself, and nobody is expected to hold all 22 in equal measure. Read as a checklist they would only produce discouragement, which is the opposite of what they exist for.

The useful way to read them is one at a time. Availability, for instance, is a real question for anyone helping others while holding down a job, and Cautiousness is a genuine tension for a practitioner who wants to be useful quickly.

How these differ from the nine virtues

The traits overlap with the nine virtues of the Code of Character and Conduct, and the two are easy to confuse, but they are separate instruments doing separate jobs.

The nine virtues are trained and tracked: each has its own live session, and holding eight of the ten current is a condition of progressing. These 22 traits are not tracked at all. They are held up as a description of the person the framework hopes you are becoming, and examined privately rather than assessed.

Why character is named at all

Most professional training describes only what a practitioner can do. Achology also describes who they are, because in helping work the two cannot be separated: a skilled practitioner who is careless with confidences, or impatient with people who are slow to change, does harm that technique cannot offset.

That reasoning is set out in full in why Achology emphasises character development. Alongside these traits sit the commitments every practising Achologist makes to clients, and the added standards that apply while you are still training. Between them they describe the practitioner the whole pathway is trying to produce.

post_title: What is the Achology Code of Ethics (Ethical Conduct)?
old_keyword: what is the Achology Code of Ethics (Ethical Conduct)
new_seo_title: What Is the Achology Code of Ethics?
new_seo_description: The Achology Code of Ethics is the framework of professional conduct for every practising Achologist, grounded in virtue ethics.
new_body_html:
So what is the Code of Ethics, and what does it ask of you in practice? The Achology Code of Ethics is the framework of professional conduct that every practising Achologist works within. Its formal name is the Ethical Framework for Practitioners of Applied Psychology. It is the primary reference members use when making decisions about their own conduct, whether professional, relational, financial, or social, and adhering to it is a condition of standing as a member.

What it is grounded in

The framework is built on virtue ethics, the tradition running from Socrates and the Stoics through Aristotle, which emphasises cultivating good character over simply following rules. The handbook presents the code as an integrity health check rather than a box-ticking exercise, with the aim of helping members aspire to be better, not merely to do the right thing in the moment. Integrity is named its cornerstone virtue.

The three ways it is used

The code is not a document you read once and shelve. The handbook names three live uses for it: guiding everyday professional practice, including being open about it with a client at the outset; supporting ethical decision-making, giving you a structured way to weigh a real dilemma when two principles pull against each other; and supporting reflection, explicitly including the coaching and practice sessions on the pathway. In other words, it is meant to be used in the room, not admired on a shelf.

How it is trained and kept current

The code comes with a six-part video training course, working through moral and ethical excellence, the role of an ethically minded Achologist, the integrity health check, ongoing character development, the qualities that positively influence people, and a closing commitment to keep the practice alive. Attending the live Code of Ethics training once a year is a continuing professional development (CPD) compliance requirement from Achologist Adept onward. It is one of Achology's three conduct codes, distinct from the Code of Character and Conduct and the Community Code of Conduct. Its values are expressed in more usable form as the ten value commitments and the nine value-based principles.

post_title: What are the ten core value commitments of Achology?
old_keyword: what are the ten core value commitments of Achology
new_seo_title: Achology's Ten Value Commitments
new_seo_description: Achology's ten value commitments come from its Code of Ethics, from upholding human dignity to ensuring affordable access to training.
new_body_html:
So what does Achology actually commit itself to? Ten value commitments, set out in its Code of Ethics, which bind the organisation and its members alike. They shape the goals Achology sets and the decisions it makes.

The ten commitments

  • Upholding human rights, individuality and dignity for all.
  • Actively supporting people in relieving personal suffering and distress.
  • Promoting the wellbeing, personal growth and capabilities of individuals.
  • Enhancing the quality of relationships between people, built on trust and understanding.
  • Strengthening personal resilience and effectiveness.
  • Encouraging people to embody virtuous and ethical characteristics in their interactions.
  • Maintaining the confidentiality of people's private information, prioritising their safety and wellbeing.
  • Upholding the integrity of the practitioner and client relationship in applied psychology.
  • Enhancing the usefulness of abstract psychological knowledge in practical, everyday applications.
  • Ensuring equitable and affordable access to training in applied psychology.

Where you can actually see them

A list of values is worth only as much as the things it visibly produces, so it is fair to ask where each one shows up.

The confidentiality commitment is the root of the privacy positions across the policies, and of the confidentiality standard every practising Achologist commits to with clients.

The applied-knowledge commitment, the ninth, is why the platform is built around practice rather than study alone, and why progression past the first level requires demonstrated practice rather than more completed courses.

The access commitment, the tenth, is the most visible of all. It is why the Knowledge Hub is free to read, why the free membership tier gives real access rather than a preview, and why members deliver complimentary coaching to people outside the community.

Why publish them at all

Published commitments are checkable in a way private values never are. Anyone can read the tenth commitment and then look at what Achology charges for and what it gives away, and judge whether the two match. Values kept internal cannot be tested that way, which is most of the reason for putting them in a public document.

How they fit the wider framework

The ten value commitments sit alongside the nine value-based principles, which turn these beliefs into a method for weighing a real decision, and the five community principles, which express them in daily conduct between members.

Read together they say one thing in three registers: what Achology believes, how it decides, and how members behave.

post_title: What are the seven signs of maturity that Achology teaches?
old_keyword: what are the seven signs of maturity that Achology teaches
new_seo_title: The Seven Marks of Maturity Achology Teaches
new_seo_description: Achology's seven marks of maturity describe a mature person: keeping commitments, indifference to flattery, humility, and character-led decisions.
new_body_html:
So what does Achology mean when it calls someone mature? The seven marks of maturity come from the Code of Ethics, in a section on the essence of maturity, and they describe a mature person as someone whose decisions are rooted in values rather than in passing emotions or opinions. They give members a picture of the character the whole framework is trying to help them grow toward.

The seven marks

  • Keeps long-term commitments, delaying gratification and honouring commitments even when they are uninspiring.
  • Is indifferent to flattery or criticism, holding a secure identity that is not shaken by external opinion.
  • Possesses a spirit of humility, honouring others and acknowledging their contributions.
  • Makes decisions based on character, acting proactively rather than looking for excuses.
  • Can prioritise self last, contributing to others' wellbeing in a balanced, discerning way.
  • Seeks wisdom before acting, keeping a teachable spirit and valuing counsel from the wise.
  • Consistently expresses gratitude.

What they are describing

Notice what is absent from that list. There is nothing about age, qualifications, confidence or success. Every one of the seven is about where a person's decisions come from when circumstances are not helping.

The second is the one members most often stop at. Indifference to flattery or criticism does not mean not caring what anyone thinks. It means holding an identity steady enough that praise does not inflate it and criticism does not collapse it, which for anyone who intends to sit with other people's difficulties is not a luxury but a working requirement.

Why maturity is written into an ethical framework at all

Because in helping work, technique is not the thing that fails first. A practitioner who needs the client's approval, who cannot delay their own gratification, or who is unteachable, will make poor decisions with perfectly good methods.

That is the reasoning behind Achology treating character as trainable rather than assumed, set out in why Achology emphasises character development, and it is why the marks of maturity are offered as a description to grow into rather than a test to pass. Nobody meets all seven consistently.

How they connect to everything else

The marks are one of four related pictures of the same person. They line up with the nine value-based principles, where Maturity in Character is itself named as one of the nine, and with the 22 character traits the Code of Ethics sets out.

Where those are aspirational, the nine virtues of the Code of Character and Conduct are the strand that is actually trained and tracked, through live sessions on a rolling requirement. Read together they say the same thing in four registers: what to aspire to, what to decide by, what to become, and what gets practised.

post_title: What are my commitments as a practising Achologist?
old_keyword: what are my commitments as a practising Achologist
new_seo_title: The Commitments of a Practising Achologist
new_seo_description: The commitments of a practising Achologist are five ethical standards: client needs first, competence, honouring relationships, and confidentiality.
new_body_html:
So what exactly are you committing to when you start working with clients? The commitments of a practising Achologist are five ethical standards taken on when serving the public, which come from the Achology Code of Ethics. Meeting them is a condition of standing as a member.

The five commitments

  • Always put the client's needs first, ahead of your own interests.
  • Work to a high standard, keeping your professional development current so your practice stays sharp.
  • Work within your competencies, and be honest about them in relation to a client's situation.
  • Maintain healthy, honouring relationships, held with unconditional positive regard, authenticity and empathy.
  • Maintain confidentiality, privacy and trust, never disclosing a client's information without consent or genuine necessity.

The third one is the difficult one

Four of the five read as things any decent practitioner would agree to without argument. Working within your competencies is the one that costs something, because it means saying no.

Somebody arrives with a difficulty that is outside what you are trained for, or beyond what coaching can reach. They are in front of you, they want help, and you could try. The commitment says be honest about your competence in relation to their situation, which in practice means telling them this is not the right place and, where you can, saying where might be.

That is also why the second commitment exists alongside it. Keeping your development current is what widens the range of situations you can genuinely take on, rather than widening what you are willing to attempt.

What sits alongside the five

The code adds several practical duties. When you offer services to the public you make sure appropriate insurance is in place, and you hold the same standards whether you work online or in person. You are also expected to be accountable, meaning ready to explain how you have met your obligations if asked.

All of it exists for one purpose: protecting the client's interests and their capacity to decide for themselves. That last part matters. The commitments are not written to make you cautious. They are written so the person in front of you stays the one making decisions about their own life.

How these connect to the rest of the framework

The five commitments are the Code of Ethics in its most usable form, expressing the same values as the ten value commitments and the nine value-based principles, which are what you reach for when two obligations pull against each other.

They assume the character traits expected of an Achologist, they are kept current through annual ethics training, and they apply with added care while you are still training, which the standards for a trainee Achologist sets out.

post_title: Which professional standards apply to a trainee Achologist?
old_keyword: which professional standards apply to a trainee Achologist
new_seo_title: The Standards for a Trainee Achologist
new_seo_description: The standards for a trainee Achologist include telling clients of trainee status, anonymising client work, and meeting the same ethical standards.
new_body_html:
So what is expected of you while you are still training? The standards for a trainee Achologist apply to members still working through a practitioner qualification course, who hold to the same ethical framework as qualified members, with a few added responsibilities that reflect where they are. The central one is honesty about status: a trainee tells clients, or makes sure they know, that they are training.

What trainees commit to

  • Tell clients you are a trainee. After qualifying, whether to disclose past trainee status becomes a matter of professional judgement.
  • Get permission before using any client work for educational purposes, with identities thoroughly anonymised, and treat consent as mandatory wherever anonymity cannot be guaranteed.
  • Provide services that meet the framework's professional, moral and ethical standards.
  • Work with reasonable care and skill, collaborating with senior practitioners and professional advisors.
  • Stay mindful of any conflict between obligations, such as to other clients or to a training provider, and seek guidance.
  • Talk honestly with trusted members of the community about your training, your client work and your ethical practice.

Why disclosure comes first

Of the six, telling clients you are training is the one everything else rests on, and it is the one trainees find hardest. Saying it out loud can feel like an admission of not being good enough yet.

It is the opposite. A person deciding whether to work with you is entitled to know what they are agreeing to, and a trainee who says so is demonstrating exactly the honesty the framework asks for. Most people, told plainly, are entirely willing. What they object to is finding out later.

How the pathway protects the people you practise on

The standards are not the only safeguard, which is worth knowing if practising while still learning sounds uncomfortable. The structure itself is built so that you practise on the people best able to absorb it first.

You receive coaching as a client before delivering any. Peer coaching comes next, with fellow members who understand the learning context. Only at Senior Achologist (Level One) does coaching people outside the community begin, by which point you have completed courses, been coached repeatedly and received structured feedback on your own practice.

Where these standards sit

They are additions to, not replacements for, the commitments every practising Achologist makes to clients, and they assume the character traits the community expects throughout.

Two of the six, seeking guidance and talking honestly with other members, are not restrictions at all. They describe the ordinary use of a learning community, and the mentoring available with membership is where most trainees find them.

post_title: Is there a free Achology membership tier, and what does it include?

So can you join Achology without paying anything, and what do you actually get? Yes, there is a free Achology membership tier and it needs no payment to join. What free Achology membership includes

  • The events calendar, with free events running Monday to Friday, excluding holidays.

What your first week can look like

Join a free event, post to the coaching board and apply for a session, then start reading and asking in the forum. None of that costs anything.

It is also enough to answer the question most people actually have at this stage, which is not what the features are but whether these are their kind of people and whether it is worth their time. The free tier exists so you can find that out honestly rather than from a sales page.

The free tier does not include the courses, the unlimited live sessions, or the structured mentorship. Those sit with paid Achology Membership, at $7 for the first 30 days and then $34.50 a month.

post_title: How do monthly and annual Achology memberships differ?

  • Annual: $345 per year, which works out at roughly two months free compared with paying monthly for a year, and renews annually unless you cancel before the renewal date.

Whichever plan you choose, membership is where the practising side of Achology happens: access to courses, unlimited live sessions, structured mentorship, the coaching board, daily discussion groups, and the networking that runs through it all. Which one to choose

The monthly plan, with its $7 first month, is the low-commitment way in: sensible if you want to try the community or are not yet sure how long you will stay. The annual plan is the better value if you already know you want to be part of Achology for the year, since it saves you about two months' worth of payments. post_title: My course included free membership. What happens when it ends?

new_seo_title: What Happens When Your Free Course Membership Ends?
new_seo_description: When your free course membership ends, it continues automatically at the standard monthly rate of $34.50 until you cancel it inside Circle.

So what happens when your free course membership runs out? It does not simply stop. A course purchase comes with three months of complimentary Achology Membership, and when those three months end the membership continues automatically at the standard rate of $34.50 a month until you cancel it. You can cancel at any time inside the community platform, Circle, which stops all future payments.

What you need to do, either way

  • To keep your community access: nothing. It carries on and you are billed monthly once the complimentary period ends.
  • To stop it: cancel before the three months are up, and no payment is taken.
  • Either way, the course you bought is unaffected. Cancelling stops future payments; it does not remove the lifetime access to the course itself.

Why the membership continues rather than lapsing

This is the part worth understanding rather than being caught by. The three months are not a trial of a product you might later buy. They are the community half of what you already bought, and it runs on from the first day.

Course study and community membership are two different things. The course gives you the material. The community is where the practice happens: the live events, the coaching board, the peer sessions and the mentorship that membership includes. Including three months with every course is how Achology puts the two together rather than selling study on its own, since study without practice does not produce a practitioner.

Whether that continues is genuinely your call, and it is a single click either way. Free course membership is not withdrawn without notice: it simply moves onto the standard monthly rate once the complimentary period ends.

Two things that catch people out

The complimentary period is longer with some purchases. The Access All Areas Pass includes twelve months rather than three, as do the school bundles, so the date you are watching for is not always three months out.

post_title: Which Achology events qualify for accreditation credit?

So which Achology events earn accreditation credit? Nine of Achology's 22 event types earn accreditation credit. They are the events governed by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP), the independent body that verifies members' professional development. The other 13, the general community events and mentorship groups, carry no credit in any role.

The six that earn a session credit

  • Skill Development Workshop
  • Principle-Based Reflective Discussion
  • Case Study-Based Discussion Group
  • The Coaching HOT Seat
  • Achologist-Led Tutorial
  • Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback Session

Attending one earns a Virtual Achologist Led Training Session (VALTS) credit. Hosting or taking a coaching role earns a Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit instead, because that is delivery rather than attendance.

The three that count differently

  • The Code of Ethics Training and the Code of Character and Conduct Training earn no session credit. Attending keeps your two compliance strands current, which is required for progression at all.
  • The Group Facilitation and VALTS Host Training is the gateway event: completing it qualifies you to host, and so to start earning credit for delivery.

What the other 13 are for

It would be a mistake to read the split as valuable against not valuable. The community events and mentorship groups carry no credit because they are not assessed activities, not because they matter less. They are where members find people working on the same things, and the mentorship groups in particular are where readiness to host is usually recognised.

What the distinction is actually for is honesty about the record. A credit says an independent body confirmed you did something specific, in a specific role. Attending a discussion because you enjoyed it is real, and it is not the same claim.

How to plan around it

Knowing the nine matters when you are working toward a level with a fixed requirement, since each level asks for a certain number of sessions across a certain spread of types. A year spent entirely in community events would leave your record where it started.

If you are unsure what suits where you are now, choosing the right event for your level is the practical guide, the full list of live events covers all 22, and every credit is claimed and verified afterwards rather than awarded automatically.

post_title: What steps should I follow to organise my own Achology event?

Every event uses a locked template, so each one reads consistently regardless of who is hosting. The only part you write yourself is a short Theme of This Specific Event paragraph naming what your session covers.

1. Open the Host a Live Event space on Circle and find your event in the Event Descriptions Library.

2. Copy the full template.

3. Start a direct message to a member of the Eldership team.

4. Paste the template into the message.

5. Write your Theme of This Specific Event paragraph at the top.

6. Send it. The Eldership member approves it, publishes it, and adds the event image.

That is genuinely the whole process. The template exists so that hosting your first event is a matter of describing your theme rather than designing a session from nothing.

The community events, the ones carrying no credit, sit in a second tier reached by informal invitation from the Eldership team rather than application. Readiness is recognised through sustained participation in the facilitation mentorship group and the host training. Once invited, you publish them the same way.

You are also invited to record a short takeaway from the session while still on the group call. The Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) then reviews the claim and records the credit against your account.

The steps, in order

  • Attend or host the event.
  • Record your short takeaway while still on the call, if the host invites one.
  • Submit the claim through the member self-report form, naming the event and the role you took.
  • Wait for verification. The credit appears on your record once it is confirmed, not before.

The role matters, because it decides which credit you receive: attending earns one kind, delivering or hosting another, and how the credit splits by role sets out the difference.

Why the credit is not instant

Hosts will not tell you a credit has been recorded, because at that moment it has not been. Verification is a separate step, done by somebody other than you, and it takes as long as it takes.

That delay is the process working rather than the system running slowly. No self-reported activity enters the official record until an independent body has checked it, and a record that updated the instant a member claimed something would be a record nobody had checked. What makes an Achology standing worth anything to an employer or a client is precisely that they do not have to take your word for it.

The habit that prevents trouble

Submit as you go. Unsubmitted work is invisible to the system no matter how much of it you have done, and the most common disappointment on the pathway is a member who has genuinely done the activity, whose own checklist looks healthy, and whose level does not arrive because the claims were never made.

Treat the checklist as your plan and the verified record as your score. Doing the activity is most of the effort; claiming it is what turns effort into progress.

Where the verified credit lives

Confirmed credit is added to your official record in the Achology Member Data Centre, which tracks activity across every member level. That record is what you draw on when you need to evidence your progression to somebody outside Achology, and it is what stands behind a certificate of achievement as distinct from a certificate of completion.

post_title: What does the Coaching HOT Seat entail?
old_keyword: what does the Coaching HOT Seat entail

new_seo_description: The Coaching HOT Seat is a live Achology event: one member takes the seat and is coached by up to three Achologists while others observe.
new_body_html:
So what does the Coaching HOT Seat entail, and what is it like to sit in one? The Coaching HOT Seat is one of the six Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) types, and it is a live coaching demonstration. One member takes the seat with a real challenge or goal, up to three Achologists coach them in turn, and the rest of the group observes.

What actually happens in it

The person in the seat brings something genuine they are working through, not a tidy example invented for practice. The coaching then happens in real time, in front of everyone.

That is what makes it valuable and slightly daunting in equal measure. For the observers, watching skilled coaching up close, and seeing how a good coach handles a real person, is one of the fastest ways to improve their own practice. It also shows the difference between coaching heard about in a workshop and coaching watched happening in real time, with all the pauses, wrong turns and corrections a tidy example would edit out.

Up to three Achologists coach in turn, so you also see different styles brought to the same problem, and how each reads the person in front of them slightly differently.

What it is like to sit in the seat

Taking the seat yourself is the part members are often nervous about and glad they did. You bring a real issue and receive focused coaching from several practitioners, with the group's attention on the work rather than on you.

Most people find it far more supportive than exposing, and leave with something they can actually use. Knowing that up to three Achologists are working on the same issue in turn, rather than one voice alone, is usually what settles any early nerves about taking the seat.

How credit works

The roles earn different credit. The coaches earn a Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit for coaching, the person in the seat earns a PALS received, and the observers earn a VALTS credit for attending.

Why members rate it

Coaching in public asks a different quality of performance than a private session: you cannot hide a hesitation, and you see how others handle the same moment. That is why the HOT Seat is one of the alternative PALS formats required at the senior levels, and why many members point to it as where their coaching genuinely sharpened. Once qualified, you can host your own, and it counts among the events that earn accreditation credit.

post_title: What are the major milestones in Achology's history?

So what are the milestones in Achology's history? Achology's history begins in 2012, when Kain Ramsay published what is described as the world's first video-based psychology course. The learning platform itself was founded in 2014, and the original company, the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology, was founded in 2017.

From there it grew into a global applied-psychology platform with more than 670,000 students in its database today. The milestones below are less a list of dates than a single, consistent direction: from one course, toward a global, accredited, community-based way of learning.

The milestones along the way

  • 2012: the world's first video-based psychology course is published, the foundation of what became Achology.
  • 2014: the Achology learning platform is founded, with 12 courses.
  • 2015: the curriculum expands to 17 interlinked courses.
  • 2016: live online skill and competency development workshops begin, the first sign of the community model to come.
  • 2017: a landmark year, reaching 100,000 students, with a bespoke platform build begun and the exclusive Skilled Helper course launched with Prof. Gerard Egan.
  • 2019: the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP), the flagship course, launches.
  • 2020: the shift to online learning accelerates worldwide, and the platform meets the demand at scale.
  • 2021: the community learning system is upgraded and gains continuing professional development (CPD) accreditation, with 350,000 total enrolled students.
  • 2022: half a million students reached worldwide, with the curriculum grown to 25 courses.
  • 2023: the version 2 community portal launches with the current 28-course curriculum.
  • 2024: the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) is founded by Master Achologists, to raise integrity standards in the field.
  • 2025: a full migration to Circle gives Achology its permanent online home.
  • 2025 to 2026: an Eldership team is established and free learning is opened to the public, with 670,000+ students in the database.

How to read the dates

post_title: What happens in a principle-based reflective discussion?
old_keyword: what happens in a principle-based reflective discussion
new_seo_title: Principle-Based Reflective Discussion Explained
new_seo_description: A principle-based reflective discussion is a 90-minute Achology group session that works one principle through questions and applies it to practice.
new_body_html:
So what happens in a principle-based reflective discussion? It is a 90-minute group session built around a single principle, worked through a set of questions and applied to your own life and practice rather than discussed in the abstract. You leave with a position on it you did not have when you arrived, and usually with the reasons you had not examined.

How a session works

The host opens with one principle and a small number of questions written to open it up. There is no lecture and no correct destination.

Members answer in turn, and the value sits in the difference between the answers. One person has lived the principle and found it costly, another has only read it, a third has quietly ignored it for years. Hearing all three at once does something reading cannot: it shows you which parts of your own understanding are borrowed and which you have actually tested.

Why a whole session for one principle

Because a principle held loosely fails at exactly the moment it matters.

Applied psychology is not short of principles, and most people can recite plenty. Under pressure, in a real conversation with a real person in difficulty, the ones that hold are the ones you have examined against your own conduct. That examination is uncomfortable enough that nobody does it alone by accident, which is why it gets a scheduled session and a group.

This is also the format that asks least of a newcomer. There is nothing to perform and no technique to demonstrate, so a member of Achology who has not yet coached anybody can take a full part in one on their first week, which is not true of the practice formats.

Where it fits among the other sessions

It is one of six session types that carry accreditation credit, and each builds a different muscle. Skill development workshops rehearse a technique. Case study discussion groups read a situation. The Coaching HOT Seat puts real coaching in front of observers. The principle-based reflective discussion sits underneath all of them, on the thinking the other formats assume you have already done.

All six run to the same 90 minutes, and if you are unsure which to start with, there is a guide to choosing the right event level.

Attending and claiming credit

Sessions appear in the Upcoming Events calendar at community.achology.com; RSVP and join as you would for any other event. Attending earns one Virtual Achologist Led Training Session (VALTS) credit, and hosting earns one Peer-to-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit, as set out in the list of which events earn accreditation credit.

Members can host this format themselves once they reach the first accreditation level and complete the group facilitation and hosting training, with no further approval needed. Hosting your own event covers what that involves.

Why this matters beyond Achology

Every helping profession runs some version of this, under different names: supervision, reflective practice, case consultation. They exist because the work asks people to act on principles under pressure, and a principle you have never argued about with anyone is not yet yours.

What the format protects against is the thing that quietly ends careers in helping work: a practitioner who has learned the words for what they do without ever testing whether they believe them. That is worth 90 minutes, whether or not you ever collect the credit.
